column1: What is the fundamental physical process occurring when a saw tooth cuts wood fiber?
column2: Orthogonal cutting via controlled shear failure: compressive stress builds ahead of the tooth's rake face until shear strength along the grain is exceeded, causing a chip to separate.

column1: What are the three structural axes that define wood's anisotropy, and why do they matter for milling?
column2: Longitudinal (grain direction), radial (rays from pith), and tangential (growth rings) — they dictate cutting mechanics, dimensional stability, and commercial board value.

column1: How does kerf width directly impact sawmill yield, using bandsaw vs. circular saw as an example?
column2: A 0.045in bandsaw kerf removes less than a quarter of the material a 0.187in circular saw kerf removes; across 12 cuts on a 20ft log this is ~0.52 board feet/log difference, scaling to ~26,000 board feet annually at 200 logs/day.

column1: Why does thinner saw blade kerf trade off against cut quality?
column2: Thinner blades deflect more under cutting forces, producing wavy cut surfaces that require additional planing, which reduces net yield despite saving kerf material.

column1: What is the key structural difference between softwood tracheids and hardwood cell architecture?
column2: Softwood tracheids perform both conductive and structural roles simultaneously; hardwoods separate these functions into large vessel elements (pores) for water transport and dense fiber cells for structural support.

column1: What is Microfibril Angle (MFA) and how does it differ between juvenile and mature wood?
column2: MFA is the orientation angle of cellulose microfibrils in the S2 cell wall layer. Juvenile wood has high MFA (30-45°), making it flexible but less stiff; mature wood has low MFA (5-15°), producing higher stiffness-to-weight ratio.

column1: Which cell wall layer dominates the mechanical behavior of wood fiber, and why?
column2: The S2 (middle secondary wall) layer, because it is by far the thickest layer and its microfibril angle determines overall stiffness and flexibility of the cell.

column1: What is the difference between ring-porous and diffuse-porous hardwoods?
column2: Ring-porous species (oak, ash) have dramatically larger earlywood pores than latewood, creating strong figure; diffuse-porous species (maple, cherry) have roughly consistent pore sizes across the growth ring.

column1: Why is primary log breakdown considered an 'irreversible act of geometric commitment'?
column2: Each kerf pass permanently fixes board dimensions, grain orientation, figure exposure, and structural integrity — unlike machining, material removed during milling cannot be reclaimed or redefined.

column1: What are typical radial vs. tangential shrinkage rates in green lumber, and why does this matter for milling?
column2: Radial shrinkage is 3-8%, tangential shrinkage is 6-12% depending on species; this asymmetry requires milling oversize by calculated margins and dictates grain orientation choices (quartersawn vs flatsawn) for dimensional stability.

column1: How does quartersawn grain orientation differ from flatsawn in terms of performance tradeoffs?
column2: Quartersawn boards (rings perpendicular to face) resist cupping/twist and reveal ray fleck figure but yield less width; flatsawn boards (tangential ring orientation) maximize width yield but exhibit greater seasonal movement.

column1: Why does blade dullness cause exponential rather than linear increases in cutting energy and cost?
column2: A degraded rake angle (e.g., 15° to 8°) turns the blade into a wedge that must both cut and hydraulically displace fibers simultaneously, compounding mechanical work, heat generation, motor load, and reducing grade recovery by one or two quality tiers.
